title: Between the two
hookLine: when they spend, neither wasteful nor stingy, but in between (25:67)

lines: THE ONE WHO WON'T BUY A SANDWICH.
cards: There are two kinds of people who are hard to go shopping with. One buys everything: the second pair of shoes, the upgrade, the thing on sale, and checks the bank balance with one eye closed.
The other won't buy a sandwich, counts every coin twice, and somehow makes everyone around them feel guilty for eating. Some people manage to be both in the same week.
The portrait of the servants of the Merciful continues, and one of its strokes is about money.

teach.b: Verse sixty-seven. Pickthall: "And those who, when they spend, are neither prodigal nor grudging; and there is ever a firm station between the two".
Prodigal is israf: going past the limit, spending beyond what's needed or right.
Grudging is qatr: tightening, squeezing, holding back what ought to be given.

Between them, qawam, Pickthall's firm station. It comes from the same root as qama, to stand upright: the place where something stands steady, not tipping either way. So the middle here isn't lukewarm.

It's upright. Another surah gives the same picture with a body: don't keep your hand chained to your neck, and don't stretch it out all the way either. And a moment in Bukhari shows the middle in a real decision.
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas was ill and thought he might die. He was wealthy, with one daughter as his heir. He asked the Prophet ﷺ if he could give two-thirds of his wealth away in charity.
No, he was told. Half? No.

teach.h: A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.
teach.b: A third, the Prophet said, and a third is a lot. Better to leave your heirs well off than dependent on other people. Even generosity has a middle.
The question isn't only, am I giving enough? It's also, am I keeping enough for the people I'm responsible for? The firm station is where both get a fair answer.
And it isn't a single number. It moves with your life.

how: Muslim teachers cite 25:67 and 17:29 on balanced spending, and Islamic law generally limits bequests to one third of an estate, following the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

o: a fixed share of wealth owed to the poor each year
a promise to give away all you own to charity
a firm, upright middle between wasting and hoarding

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: the middle in 25:67 means being lukewarm
qawam comes from standing upright: a steady, balanced place.
the Prophet told Sa'd that a third is a lot
a third, and a third is a lot; better to leave heirs well off.
the verse only warns against stinginess
it names both: neither prodigal nor grudging.

games.q: you're Sa'd, ill and wealthy, with one daughter as your heir. you ask to give two-thirds of your wealth to charity. what's the answer?
o: no; a third, and a third is a lot.
no; give nothing until you've recovered.
games.why: two-thirds, no. half, no. a third, and a third is a lot. better to leave your heirs well off than dependent on others.

practice: Think of something you bought this week, or are about to buy, and ask whether it's past what you need, or what's right.
Then the other side: are you holding back somewhere you should be giving, to yourself, your family, someone in need? Don't scold yourself; just look for where the firm middle would stand.

wordCard.voice: Qawam. A firm, upright station between prodigal and grudging spending, standing steady, not tipping either way. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: qawam, a firm, upright middle; from the root of qama, to stand.

carryVoice: Your line: in between. The middle here isn't lukewarm; it's upright. That's day four hundred ninety-nine.

sources.q: And those who, when they spend, are neither prodigal nor grudging; and there is ever a firm station between the two
